danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 4
paragraphs: Pavlograd-husarerne lå to mil fra Braunau. Den eskadron, hvori Nikolaj Rostov (kadet) gjorde tjeneste, var indkvarteret i den tyske landsby Salzeneck. De bedste kvarterer i landsbyen var tildelt ritmester Denisov, eskadronschefen, kendt i hele kavaleridivisionen som Vaska Denisov. Kadet Rostov havde, lige siden han indhentede regimentet i Polen, boet sammen med eskadronschefen.

Den 11. oktober, den dag da alt var i oprør ved hovedkvarteret over nyheden om Macks nederlag, forløb lejrlivet blandt eskadronens officerer som sædvanligt. Denisov, der havde tabt ved kortspil hele natten, var endnu ikke kommet hjem, da Rostov vendte tidligt tilbage fra en fouragering. Rostov red i sin kadetuniform op til indgangen, svang med ungdommelig smidighed benet over sadlen, stod et øjeblik i stigbøjlen, som om han nødigt ville skilles fra sin hest, og sprang endelig ned og kaldte på sin oppasser.

»Nå, Bondarenko, min kære!« sagde han til husaren, der stormede hovedkulds hen til hesten. »Gå ham op og ned, min gode ven,« fortsatte han med den glade, broderlige hjertelighed, som godmodige unge mennesker viser alle, når de er lykkelige.
»Jawohl, Deres Eksellence,« svarede ukraineren muntert og kastede med hovedet.
»Husk nu, gå ham godt op og ned!«

En anden husar styrtede også hen mod hesten, men Bondarenko havde allerede kastet trensens tøjler over hestens hoved. Det var tydeligt, at kadetten var gavmild med drikkepenge, og at det betalte sig at betjene ham. Rostov klappede hesten på halsen og derefter på flanken og nølede et øjeblik.

»Pragtfuldt! Sikke en hest det bliver!« tænkte han med et smil, og med sablen holdt op og sporerne klirrende løb han op ad trappen til indgangen. Hans vært, der i vest og spids hue, med en høtyv i hånden, var i færd med at rydde gødning fra kostalden, kiggede ud, og hans ansigt lyste straks op ved synet af Rostov. »Schön gut Morgen! Schön gut Morgen!« sagde han med et blink og et lystigt smil, tydeligvis glad for at hilse den unge mand.
»Schön gut Morgen! (Rigtig god morgen!)«

»Schon fleissig? (Allerede flittig?)« sagde Rostov med det samme glade, broderlige smil, der ikke forlod hans ivrige ansigt. »Hoch Oestreicher! Hoch Russen! Kaiser Alexander hoch! (Leve Østrig! Leve russerne! Leve kejser Alexander!)« sagde han og citerede ord, den tyske vært ofte gentog.
»Allerede flittig?«
»Leve Østrig! Leve russerne! Leve kejser Alexander!«
Tyskeren lo, kom ud af kostalden, tog sin hue af og svingede den over hovedet og råbte:
»Und die ganze Welt hoch! (Og leve hele verden!)«
»Og leve hele verden!«

Rostov svingede sin hue ligesom tyskeren og råbte leende: »Und vivat die ganze Welt!« Skønt hverken tyskeren, der ryddede sin kostald, eller Rostov, der var vendt tilbage med sin deling fra fouragering, havde nogen særlig grund til at glæde sig, så de på hinanden med fornøjet henrykkelse og broderlig kærlighed, nikkede som tegn på gensidig hengivenhed og skiltes smilende — tyskeren til sin kostald og Rostov til den hytte, han delte med Denisov.
»Hvad med din herre?« spurgte han Lavrusjka, Denisovs oppasser, som hele regimentet kendte som en gavtyv.

»Ikke hjemme siden i aftes. Han har nok tabt,« svarede Lavrusjka. »Jeg kender ham efterhånden — vinder han, kommer han tidligt hjem for at prale; men bliver han borte til om morgenen, betyder det, at han har tabt og kommer hjem i et rasende humør. Skal det være kaffe?«
»Ja tak.«

Ti minutter senere bragte Lavrusjka kaffen. »Han kommer!« sagde han. »Nu bliver der ballade!« Rostov kiggede ud af vinduet og så Denisov komme hjem. Denisov var en lille mand med rødt ansigt, funklende sorte øjne og sort, filtret overskæg og hår. Han bar en uknappet kappe, vide bukser, der hang ned i folder, og en krøllet felthat på nakken. Han gik op til indgangen med sænket hoved og mørkt ansigt.
»Lavwusjka!« råbte han højt og vredt. »Tag det af, dumrian!«
»Jamen, det gør jeg jo,« lød Lavrusjkas stemme.
»Nå, du er allerede oppe,« sagde Denisov, da han kom ind i stuen.
»Længe siden,« svarede Rostov. »Jeg har allerede været ude efter hø og har set frøken Mathilde.«

»Viwkelig! Og jeg har tabt, bwor. Tabte i går som en forbandet idiot!« råbte Denisov, der ikke kunne udtale sine r'er. »Sikken uflaks! Sikken uflaks! Lige så snart du gik, begyndte det, og det blev bare ved. Hej der! Te!«
Han krympede ansigtet, men smilede alligevel og viste sine korte, stærke tænder, mens han med buttede fingre på begge hænder rodte op i sit tykke, filtrede, sorte hår.

»Og sikke en djævel der fik mig til at gå til den wotte« (en officer med tilnavnet »rotten«), sagde han og gnubbede sin pande og hele sit ansigt med begge hænder. »Bare tænk, han lod mig ikke vinde et eneste kaht, ikke ét kaht.«
Han tog den tændte pibe, der blev rakt ham, greb den i næven og bankede den i gulvet, så gnisterne fløj, mens han fortsatte med at råbe.
»Han lader én vinde på enkelt og snapper gevinsten, så snart man fordobler; giver på enkelt og tager på dobbelt!«
Han spredte den brændende tobak, knuste piben og smed den væk. Så sad han tavs et stykke tid, og pludselig kiggede han muntert på Rostov med sine funklende, sorte øjne.

»Bare vi i det mindste havde nogle kvinder her; men der er slet ingenting at lave ud over at dwikke. Bare vi snart kunne komme i kamp. Hej, hvem er der?« sagde han og vendte sig mod døren, da han hørte tunge støvler og klirrende sporer nærme sig og standse, og en ærbødig hosten.
»Eskadronens kvartermester!« sagde Lavrusjka.
Denisovs ansigt krympede sig endnu mere.
»Elendigt!« mumlede han og kastede en pung med noget guld i. »Wostov, kære ven, se lige, hvor meget der er tilbage, og stik pungen under hovedpuden,« sagde han og gik ud til kvartermesteren.
Rostov tog pengene og begyndte mekanisk at sortere de gamle og nye mønter i separate bunker og tælle dem.
»Nå! Teljanin! Goddag! De plukkede mig i nat,« lød Denisovs stemme fra det tilstødende rum.
»Hvor? Hos Bykov, hos rotten ... Det vidste jeg nok,« svarede en pibende stemme, og løjtnant Teljanin, en lille officer fra samme eskadron, kom ind i stuen.

Rostov stak pungen under puden og trykkede den fugtige lille hånd, der blev rakt ham. Teljanin var af en eller anden grund blevet overført fra garden lige inden dette felttog. Han opførte sig udmærket i regimentet, men var ikke afholdt; Rostov i særdeleshed afskyede ham og var ude af stand til at overvinde eller skjule sin grundløse antipati mod manden.
»Nå, unge rytter, hvordan opfører min Rurik sig?« spurgte han. (Rurik var en ung hest, Teljanin havde solgt til Rostov.)
Løjtnanten kiggede aldrig den, han talte med, lige i ansigtet; hans øjne vandrede ustandseligt fra den ene genstand til den anden.
»Jeg så dig ride i morges ...« tilføjede han.

»Åh, den er udmærket, en god hest,« svarede Rostov, skønt hesten, han havde betalt syv hundrede rubler for, ikke var halvdelen værd. »Den er begyndt at halte lidt på det venstre forben,« tilføjede han.
»Hoven er revnet! Det er ingenting. Jeg skal vise dig, hvad man gør, og hvilken slags nitte man bruger.«
»Ja tak, gør det,« sagde Rostov.
»Jeg skal vise dig, jeg skal vise dig! Det er ingen hemmelighed. Og det er en hest, du vil takke mig for.«
»Så lad mig få den hentet,« sagde Rostov, der gerne ville undgå Teljanin, og gik ud for at give ordren.

I gangen sad Denisov med en pibe på hug på tærsklen over for kvartermesteren, der aflagde rapport. Da han fik øje på Rostov, krympede Denisov ansigtet, pegede med tommelfingeren over skulderen ind mod det rum, hvor Teljanin sad, rynkede panden og rystede sig af væmmelse.
»Uf! Jeg kan ikke lide den fyr,« sagde han uden hensyn til kvartermesterens tilstedeværelse.
Rostov trak på skuldrene, som ville han sige: »Det kan jeg heller ikke, men hvad skal man gøre?« og efter at have givet sin ordre vendte han tilbage til Teljanin.
Teljanin sad i den samme slappe stilling, som Rostov havde forladt ham i, og gnubbede sine små, hvide hænder.
»Sikke nogle modbydelige mennesker, der findes,« tænkte Rostov, da han kom ind.
»Har du sagt, de skal bringe hesten?« spurgte Teljanin, rejste sig og så ligegyldigt om sig.
»Ja.«
»Lad os selv gå ud. Jeg kom egentlig bare for at spørge Denisov om gårsdagens ordre. Har du fået den, Denisov?«
»Ikke endnu. Men hvor skal du hen?«
»Jeg vil lære den unge mand her at sko en hest,« sagde Teljanin.
De gik ud gennem indgangen og hen i stalden. Løjtnanten viste, hvordan man nittede hoven, og gik så til sine egne kvarterer.
Da Rostov gik tilbage, stod der en flaske vodka og en pølse på bordet. Denisov sad og kradse med sin pen på et stykke papir. Han kiggede mørkt på Rostov og sagde: »Jeg skwiver til hende.«
Han lænede albuerne på bordet med pennen i hånden og var tydeligvis glad for chancen til hurtigere at sige i ord, hvad han ville skrive, og fortalte Rostov indholdet af sit brev.

»Ser du, min ven,« sagde han, »vi sover, når vi ikke elsker. Vi er støvets børn ... men man forelsker sig, og man er en gud, man er wen som på skabelsens første dag ... Hvem er det nu? Send ham ad helvede til, jeg har travlt!« råbte han til Lavrusjka, der gik hen til ham uden den mindste forlegenhed.
»Hvem skulle det vel være? Du sagde jo selv, han skulle komme. Det er kvartermesteren for pengene.«
Denisov rynkede panden og var ved at råbe et svar, men standsede.
»Elendigt,« mumlede han for sig selv. »Hvor meget er der tilbage i pungen?« spurgte han og vendte sig mod Rostov.
»Syv nye og tre gamle imperialer.«
»Nåh, det er elendigt! Hvad står du der for, din fugleskræmsel? Kald på kvahtehmesteren!« råbte han til Lavrusjka.
»Denisov, lad mig låne dig noget; jeg har penge, ved du,« sagde Rostov og rødmede.
»Kan ikke lide at låne af mine egne folk, det kan jeg ikke,« brummede Denisov.
»Men hvis du ikke vil tage imod penge af mig som en kammerat, fornærmer du mig. Jeg har virkelig noget,« gentog Rostov.
»Nej, siger jeg!«
Og Denisov gik hen til sengen for at hente pungen under puden.
»Hvor har du lagt den, Wostov?«
»Under den nederste pude.«
»Den er der ikke.«
Denisov kastede begge puder på gulvet. Pungen var der ikke.
»Det er et miwakkel.«
»Vent, har du ikke tabt den?« sagde Rostov og samlede puderne op en ad gangen og rystede dem.
Han trak dynen af og rystede den. Pungen var der ikke.
»Herregud, har jeg glemt det? Nej, jeg husker, at jeg tænkte, du gemte den under dit hoved som en skat,« sagde Rostov. »Jeg lagde den lige her. Hvor er den?« spurgte han og vendte sig mod Lavrusjka.
»Jeg har ikke været i stuen. Den må ligge, hvor du lagde den.«
»Men det gør den ikke ...«
»Du gør altid det samme; du smideh ting vilkåhligt og glemmer dem. Se i dine lommer.«
»Nej, hvis jeg ikke havde tænkt på det som en skat,« sagde Rostov, »men jeg husker, at jeg lagde den der.«

Lavrusjka vendte alt sengetøjet, kiggede under sengen og under bordet, ledte overalt og blev stående midt i stuen. Denisov fulgte tavst Lavrusjkas bevægelser med øjnene, og da denne slog hænderne ud i forundring og sagde, at den var sporløst forsvundet, kiggede Denisov på Rostov.
»Wostov, du driver vel ikke skoledwengestreger ...«

Rostov mærkede Denisovs blik hvile på sig, løftede øjnene og slog dem øjeblikkeligt ned igen. Alt blodet, der syntes at have samlet sig et sted under halsen, steg til ansigtet og øjnene. Han kunne ikke trække vejret.
»Og der har ikke været andre i stuen end løjtnanten og jer selv. Det må være her et sted,« sagde Lavrusjka.
»Nå, din djævleunge, se at komme i gang og led efter den!« råbte Denisov, pludselig purpurrød, og for mod manden med en truende gestus. »Hvis pungen ikke findes, pisker jeg dig, jeg pisker jer alle!«
Rostov undveg Denisovs blik og begyndte at knappe sin frakke, spændte sablen fast og satte huen på.
»Jeg vil have den pung, siger jeg!« råbte Denisov og ruskede sin oppasser i skuldrene og stødte ham mod væggen.

»Denisov, lad ham være; jeg ved, hvem der har taget den,« sagde Rostov og gik mod døren uden at løfte øjnene. Denisov standsede, tænkte sig om et øjeblik, og da han tydeligvis forstod, hvad Rostov hentydede til, greb han hans arm.
»Vrøvl!« råbte han, og venerne på hans pande og hals stod ud som reb. »Du er gal, det siger jeg dig. Det tillader jeg ikke. Pungen er her! Jeg flår den slyngel levende, og den skal nok findes.«
»Jeg ved, hvem der har taget den,« gentog Rostov med usikker stemme og gik mod døren.
»Og jeg siger dig, du ska' ikke vove det!« råbte Denisov og styrtede hen til kadetten for at holde ham tilbage.
Men Rostov rev sin arm fri og rettede med lige så megen vrede, som om Denisov var hans værste fjende, et fast blik direkte ind i hans ansigt.
»Forstår du, hvad du siger?« sagde han med bævende stemme. »Der var ingen andre i stuen end mig. Så hvis det ikke forholder sig sådan, så ...«
Han kunne ikke fuldende sætningen og løb ud af stuen.
»Nåh, fanden ta' dig og alle de andre,« var de sidste ord, Rostov hørte.
Rostov gik til Teljanins kvarter.
»Herren er ikke hjemme, han er taget til hovedkvarteret,« sagde Teljanins oppasser. »Er der sket noget?« tilføjede han, overrasket over kadettens forpinte ansigt.
»Nej, ingenting.«
»Du har kun lige forpasset ham,« sagde oppasseren.

Hovedkvarteret lå to mil fra Salzeneck, og Rostov tog en hest og red derhen uden at vende hjem. Der var et værtshus i landsbyen, som officererne ofte besøgte. Rostov red derop og så Teljanins hest ved indgangen.
I det andet rum på værtshuset sad løjtnanten over en tallerken pølser og en flaske vin.
»Nå, er du også kommet hertil, unge mand!« sagde han smilende og løftede øjenbrynene.
»Ja,« sagde Rostov, som om det kostede ham umådelig besvær at sige det ord, og satte sig ved det nærmeste bord.
Begge var tavse. Der var to tyskere og en russisk officer i stuen. Ingen talte, og de eneste lyde var klapren af knive og løjtnantens tyggen.

Da Teljanin var færdig med sit måltid, trak han en dobbelttaske op af lommen, skilte ringene ad med sine små, hvide, opadvendte fingre, tog en guldimperial frem og rakte den med løftede øjenbryn til tjeneren.
»Skynd dig venligst,« sagde han.
Mønten var ny. Rostov rejste sig og gik hen til Teljanin.
»Må jeg se Deres pung?« sagde han med lav, næsten uhørlig stemme.
Med flakkende øjne, men stadig med løftede øjenbryn, rakte Teljanin ham pungen.
»Ja, den er pæn, den pung. Ja, ja,« sagde han og blev pludselig bleg og tilføjede: »Se på den, unge mand.«
Rostov tog pungen, undersøgte den og pengene i den og kiggede på Teljanin. Løjtnanten så sig om på sin sædvanlige vis og blev pludselig meget munter.
»Når vi kommer til Wien, kan jeg skifte den der, men i de her elendige småbyer er der ingen steder at bruge dem,« sagde han. »Nå, giv mig den, unge mand, jeg skal af sted.«
Rostov sagde ingenting.
»Og du? Skal du også have frokost? De bespiser én ganske anstændigt her,« fortsatte Teljanin. »Nå, så giv mig den.«

Han rakte hånden ud for at tage pungen. Rostov slap den. Teljanin tog pungen og begyndte ligegyldigt at putte den i lommen på sine ridebukser med løftede øjenbryn og let åben mund, som ville han sige: »Ja, ja, jeg putter min pung i lommen, og det er ganske enkelt og angår ingen andre.«
»Nå, unge mand?« sagde han med et suk og kiggede fra under sine løftede bryn ind i Rostovs øjne.
Et glimt som af et elektrisk lyn skød fra Teljanins øjne til Rostovs og tilbage, og tilbage igen i ét nu.
»Kom herhen,« sagde Rostov og greb Teljanin i armen og trak ham næsten hen til vinduet. »De penge er Denisovs; du tog dem ...« hviskede han tæt ved Teljanins øre.
»Hvad? Hvad? Hvordan vover De? Hvad?« sagde Teljanin.

Men disse ord lød som et ynkeligt, fortvivlet skrig og en bøn om tilgivelse. I det øjeblik Rostov hørte dem, faldt en enorm byrde af tvivl af ham. Han var glad, og samtidig begyndte han at ynke det ulykkelige menneske foran sig; men den opgave, han havde påbegyndt, måtte fuldføres.
»Himlen alene ved, hvad folk her kan tro,« mumlede Teljanin og greb sin hue og bevægede sig mod et lille, tomt rum. »Vi må have en forklaring ...«
»Det ved jeg, og jeg kan bevise det,« sagde Rostov.
Hver muskel i Teljanins blege, rædselsslagne ansigt begyndte at bævre; hans øjne flakkede stadig fra side til side, men med sænket blik, uden at nå Rostovs ansigt, og hans hulken var hørbar.
»Greve! ... Ødelæg ikke en ung mand ... her er de elendige penge, tag dem ...« Han kastede dem på bordet. »Jeg har en gammel far og mor ...«
Rostov tog pengene, undgik Teljanins blik og gik ud af stuen uden et ord. Men ved døren standsede han og gik derefter tilbage. »Åh Gud,« sagde han med tårer i øjnene, »hvordan kunne du gøre det?«
»Greve ...« sagde Teljanin og kom nærmere.
»Rør mig ikke,« sagde Rostov og trak sig tilbage. »Hvis du har brug for dem, så tag pengene.« Og han kastede pungen til ham og løb ud af værtshuset.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: The Pavlograd Hussars were stationed two miles from Braunau. The squadron in which Nikolai Rostov served as a cadet was billeted in the German village of Salzeneck. The best quarters in the village had been assigned to the squadron commander, cavalry captain Denisov, known throughout the entire cavalry division as Vaska Denisov. Cadet Rostov had been living with the squadron commander ever since catching up with the regiment in Poland.

On October 11 — the same day headquarters was buzzing with the news of Mack's defeat — life in this squadron's officers' quarters went on as usual. Denisov, who had been losing at cards all night, still hadn't come home when Rostov returned early that morning from a foraging expedition. In his cadet uniform, Rostov rode up to the porch with a jerk of the reins, swung his leg over the saddle with a supple, youthful motion, paused for a moment in the stirrup as though reluctant to part from his horse, then finally sprang down and called for his orderly.

"Ah, Bondarenko, my friend!" he said to the hussar who came running headlong toward the horse. "Walk him for me, there's a good fellow," he went on, with the open, brotherly warmth that good-natured young people radiate to everyone around them when they're happy.
"Yes, Your Excellency," the Ukrainian replied cheerfully, tossing his head.
"And make sure you walk him properly!"

Another hussar rushed toward the horse too, but Bondarenko had already looped the snaffle reins over its head. It was clear the cadet tipped generously and that serving him paid well. Rostov patted the horse's neck, then its flank, and lingered a moment longer.

"Wonderful! He's going to be a superb horse," he thought, smiling, and with his saber at his side and spurs jingling, he ran up the porch steps. His German landlord, wearing a waistcoat and a pointed cap and holding a pitchfork, was shoveling manure from the cow shed. His face brightened the moment he saw Rostov. [speaking in German] "Good morning! Very good morning!" he said, winking with a cheerful smile, clearly pleased to see the young man.
"A very good morning! A very good morning!"

[speaking in German] "Busy already?" Rostov replied with that same bright, brotherly smile that never left his eager face. [speaking in German] "Long live Austria! Long live Russia! Long live Emperor Alexander!" he added, repeating a phrase the German landlord used constantly.
"Busy already?"
"Hurrah for the Austrians! Hurrah for the Russians! Hurrah for Emperor Alexander!"
The German laughed, came out of the cow shed, pulled off his cap, and waved it over his head, shouting:
[speaking in German] "And long live the whole world!"
"And hurrah for the whole world!"

Rostov waved his cap in the air just like the German and laughed: [speaking in German] "And long live the whole world!" Though neither the German shoveling his cow shed nor Rostov returning from hay-gathering duty had any particular reason to rejoice, they looked at each other with joyful delight and brotherly affection, wagged their heads as a sign of mutual goodwill, and parted smiling — the German going back to his cow shed, Rostov heading to the cottage he shared with Denisov.
"Where's the master?" he asked Lavrusha, Denisov's orderly, known throughout the regiment as a rogue.

"Hasn't been back since last night. Must've been losing," Lavrusha answered. "I can always tell by now — when he wins, he comes home early to brag about it. When he stays out until morning, it means he lost, and he'll come back in a foul mood. Want coffee?"
"Yes, bring some."

Ten minutes later Lavrusha brought the coffee. "He's coming!" he announced. "Now there'll be trouble!" Rostov looked out the window and saw Denisov approaching. Denisov was a small man with a red face, sparkling black eyes, and a black tangle of mustache and hair. He wore an unbuttoned cloak, baggy trousers hanging in creases, and a crumpled shako shoved to the back of his head. He came up to the porch gloomily, his head hanging.
"Lavwuska!" he shouted, loudly and angrily. "Take this off, you blockhead!"
"I am taking it off," Lavrusha's voice came back.
"Ah — you're up already," said Denisov, walking into the room.
"Long ago," Rostov answered. "I've already been out for the hay and had a look at Fräulein Mathilde."

"Weally! And I've been losing, bwother. Lost last night like an absolute fool!" Denisov cried. He couldn't pronounce his r's. "Such wotten luck! Such wotten luck. The minute you left, it started — and it just kept going. Hey! Tea!"
Scrunching up his face in what was partly a grimace and partly a grin, showing his short, strong teeth, he began raking both sets of stubby fingers through his thick, matted black hair.

"What devil made me go to that wat?" — "the rat" being an officer's nickname — he said, rubbing his forehead and his whole face with both hands. "Can you believe it — he didn't let me win a single cahd! Not one cahd!"
He grabbed the lit pipe someone offered him, clamped it in his fist, and banged it against the floor, sending sparks flying, all while continuing to shout.
"He lets you win the singles, then snatches it back the second you double! Gives you the singles, grabs the doubles!"
He scattered the burning tobacco, smashed the pipe, and hurled it away. Then he went quiet, and suddenly looked up at Rostov with his glittering black eyes, cheerful again.

"If at least there were some women around. But there's nothing to do here but dwink. If only we could get to the fighting! Hey — who's there?" he said, turning toward the door at the sound of heavy boots, clinking spurs, and a respectful cough.
"The squadron quartermaster!" Lavrusha announced.
Denisov's face puckered even more.

"Wotten!" he muttered, tossing down a purse with some gold coins in it. "Wostov, dear fellow, count what's left and stick the purse under the pillow," he said, and went out to deal with the quartermaster.
Rostov picked up the money and, mechanically sorting the old coins from the new ones into separate piles, began counting.
"Hey, Telyanin! How are you? They cleaned me out last night," Denisov's voice came from the next room.
"Where? At Bykov's? The rat's? I knew it," a thin voice replied, and Lieutenant Telyanin — a small officer from the same squadron — walked in.

Rostov shoved the purse under the pillow and shook the moist little hand Telyanin offered. Telyanin had been transferred out of the Guards just before this campaign. He conducted himself well enough in the regiment but wasn't liked. Rostov in particular couldn't stand him, and was unable to overcome — or even hide — his baseless dislike of the man.
"Well, young cavalryman, how's my Rook doing?" Telyanin asked. Rook was a young horse he had sold to Rostov.
The lieutenant never looked directly at the person he was talking to — his eyes constantly wandered from one object to another.
"I saw you riding this morning," he added.
"Oh, he's fine — good horse," Rostov answered, even though the horse he'd paid seven hundred rubles for wasn't worth half that. "He's started going a bit lame on the left foreleg, though."
"Cracked hoof — that's nothing. I'll teach you what to do. I'll show you the right kind of rivet."
"Yes, please do," said Rostov.
"I'll show you, I'll show you. It's no secret. And you'll thank me for that horse."
"Then I'll have him brought around," said Rostov, wanting to get away from Telyanin, and he went out to give the order.

In the hallway, Denisov was squatting on the threshold with a pipe, facing the quartermaster, who was making his report. Seeing Rostov, Denisov screwed up his face, jerked his thumb over his shoulder toward the room where Telyanin sat, and gave a shudder of disgust.
"Ugh! I can't stand that fellow," he said, not caring that the quartermaster was right there.
Rostov shrugged as if to say: Neither can I, but what can you do? He gave his order and went back to Telyanin.
Telyanin sat in the same lazy posture Rostov had left him in, rubbing his small white hands.
"There really are some revolting people in this world," Rostov thought as he walked in.
"Have you told them to bring the horse?" Telyanin asked, getting up and glancing around with his usual restless casualness.
"I have."
"Let's go look ourselves. I really only stopped by to ask Denisov about yesterday's order. Did you get it, Denisov?"
"Not yet. But where are you headed?"
"I want to show this young man how to shoe a horse properly," Telyanin said.
They went through the entrance and into the stable. The lieutenant demonstrated how to set the rivet, then left for his own quarters.

When Rostov came back, there was a bottle of vodka and a sausage on the table. Denisov was sitting there, pen scratching across a sheet of paper. He looked up at Rostov gloomily and said: "I'm witing to her."
He propped his elbows on the table, pen in hand, and — clearly glad of the chance to say aloud what he wanted to put on paper — began telling Rostov the contents of his letter.

"You see, my fwiend," he said, "when we don't love, we're asleep. We're children of the dust... but the moment you fall in love — you become a god, you're as pure as on the first day of creation... Who's that now? Tell him to go to hell — I'm busy!" he shouted at Lavrusha, who came up to him without the slightest embarrassment.
"Who do you think? You told him to come yourself. It's the quartermaster — he wants the money."
Denisov frowned and started to shout something, then stopped.
"Wotten business," he muttered. "How much is left in the purse?" he asked, turning to Rostov.
"Seven new imperials and three old ones."
"Ugh — wotten! Well, what are you standing there gawking for, you scawecwow? Go call the quahtehmasteh!" he shouted at Lavrusha.
"Denisov, please — let me lend you some. I've got money, you know," said Rostov, blushing.
"Don't like bowwowing from my own comrades," Denisov growled.
"But if you won't take money from me as a friend, you'll hurt my feelings. I really do have some," Rostov insisted.
"No, I said."
Denisov went to the bed to retrieve the purse from under the pillow.
"Where did you put it, Wostov?"
"Under the bottom pillow."
"It's not here."
Denisov threw both pillows onto the floor. The purse was gone.
"That's stwange."
"Wait — maybe you dropped it?" said Rostov, picking up the pillows one by one and shaking them.
He yanked off the blanket and shook it out. No purse.
"Good lord, could I have forgotten? No — I remember thinking you were guarding it under your head like treasure," said Rostov. "I put it right here. Where is it?" He turned to Lavrusha.
"I haven't been in the room. It should be wherever you put it."
"But it's not there."
"You're always like that — you toss things down anywhere and then forget. Check your pockets."
"No — if I hadn't been thinking of it as treasure," said Rostov, "but I distinctly remember putting it there."

Lavrusha turned all the bedding inside out, looked under the bed and under the table, searched everywhere, then stood in the middle of the room and threw up his hands — it was nowhere to be found. Denisov watched Lavrusha's every move in silence, and when the orderly gave up with a helpless gesture, Denisov turned his gaze on Rostov.
"Wostov — you haven't been playing some schoolboy twick..."

Rostov felt Denisov's eyes fixed on him. He looked up and instantly dropped his gaze again. All the blood that seemed to have been pooled somewhere below his throat rushed to his face and eyes. He couldn't breathe.
"And nobody's been in the room except the lieutenant and the two of you. It has to be here somewhere," said Lavrusha.

"Now then, you little devil — get moving and find it!" Denisov shouted, suddenly turning purple and lunging at the orderly with a threatening fist. "If that purse doesn't turn up, I'll flog you — I'll flog every last one of you!"
Rostov, avoiding Denisov's eyes, began buttoning his coat, buckling on his saber, and putting on his cap.
"I want that purse, do you hear me!" Denisov bellowed, grabbing his orderly by the shoulders and slamming him against the wall.

"Denisov, leave him alone. I know who took it," said Rostov, walking toward the door without looking up. Denisov stopped, thought for a second, and — clearly understanding what Rostov was hinting at — seized his arm.

"That's nonsense!" he shouted. The veins on his forehead and neck stood out like cords. "You've lost your mind, I tell you. I won't allow it. The purse is here! I'll skin this scoundwel alive, and it'll turn up."
"I know who took it," Rostov repeated, his voice unsteady, and headed for the door.
"And I'm telling you — don't you dahe!" Denisov shouted, rushing at the cadet to hold him back.
But Rostov wrenched his arm free and, with as much fury as if Denisov were his worst enemy, fixed his eyes directly on his face.
"Do you realize what you're saying?" he asked in a shaking voice. "No one else was in this room besides me. So if the purse isn't there, then..."
He couldn't finish. He ran from the room.
"Damn it all — damn you and evewybody!" were the last words Rostov heard.
Rostov went straight to Telyanin's quarters.
"The master isn't in — he went to headquarters," Telyanin's orderly said. "Has something happened?" he added, startled by the cadet's agitated face.
"No, nothing."
"You just missed him," the orderly said.

Headquarters was two miles from Salzeneck. Without going home first, Rostov grabbed a horse and rode there. In the village there was an inn the officers frequented. Rostov rode up to it and saw Telyanin's horse tied at the porch.
In the back room of the inn, the lieutenant was sitting in front of a plate of sausages and a bottle of wine.
"Well, you've come here too, young man!" Telyanin said with a smile, raising his eyebrows.
"Yes," said Rostov, as though the word cost him enormous effort, and he sat down at the nearest table.
Neither spoke. Two Germans and a Russian officer were also in the room. Everyone was silent; the only sounds were the clatter of cutlery and Telyanin's chewing.

When Telyanin finished eating, he pulled a double purse from his pocket and, separating its rings with his small, white, upturned fingers, drew out a gold imperial. Raising his eyebrows, he handed it to the waiter.
"Quickly, please," he said.
The coin was new. Rostov stood up and walked over to Telyanin.
"May I see your purse?" he said in a low voice, barely audible.
With his eyes shifting but his eyebrows still raised, Telyanin handed over the purse.
"Yes, it's a nice purse. Yes, yes," he said, suddenly turning pale. "Take a look, young man."
Rostov took the purse, examined it and the money inside, and looked at Telyanin. The lieutenant was glancing around in his usual restless way, and suddenly seemed to grow very cheerful.
"When we get to Vienna, I'll spend it there. In these miserable little towns, there's nowhere to use it," he said. "Well — let me have it back, young man. I need to go."
Rostov said nothing.
"And you? Going to have some lunch? They feed you pretty well here," Telyanin continued. "Come on, hand it over."

He reached out for the purse. Rostov released it. Telyanin took the purse and began sliding it casually into his riding breeches pocket, his eyebrows lifted and his mouth slightly open, as if to say: Yes, I'm putting my purse in my pocket — perfectly normal, nobody's business.
"Well, young man?" he said with a sigh, glancing up from under his raised brows into Rostov's eyes.
Something like an electric spark shot between Telyanin's eyes and Rostov's — back and forth, back and forth, in a single instant.
"Come here," said Rostov, grabbing Telyanin by the arm and practically dragging him to the window. "That money belongs to Denisov — you stole it," he whispered, his mouth close to Telyanin's ear.
"What? What? How dare you? What?" Telyanin sputtered.

But the words came out as a pitiful, desperate cry — a plea for forgiveness. The instant Rostov heard them, a crushing weight of doubt fell away from him. He was relieved, and at the same time he began to pity the wretched man standing before him. But what he had started had to be finished.
"God only knows what the people here might think," Telyanin muttered, grabbing his cap and moving toward a small, empty room. "We need to talk about this..."
"I know it and I'll prove it," said Rostov.
Every muscle in Telyanin's pale, terrified face was quivering. His eyes still darted from side to side, but now they stayed low, never rising to meet Rostov's. His sobs were audible.
"Count... Don't ruin a young man's life... here — here's the wretched money, take it." He threw it on the table. "I have an old father and mother!"

Rostov picked up the money, not looking at Telyanin, and walked out of the room without a word. But at the door he stopped and turned back. "My God," he said, tears in his eyes, "how could you do this?"
"Count..." Telyanin said, stepping closer.
"Don't touch me," said Rostov, pulling away. "If you need money, take it." He flung the purse at Telyanin and ran out of the inn.
